patient.name: Femi Adebayo
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then the infectious diseases ward
patient.complaint: Fever, rigors and headache for 3 days, 10 days after returning from Lagos
background: Born in London; visited family in Nigeria for 3 weeks
Took no malaria prophylaxis: 'I grew up with it'
No past medical history, no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fever in a returned traveller (often sub-Saharan Africa) and low platelets, or 'Which is the most likely causative organism?' where severity, the blood film or relapse picks the species.

points: 3 days of fever with **shaking rigors**, then drenching sweats.
Headache, aching muscles, vomiting and loose stools.

steps.lead: Fever plus travel to **sub-Saharan Africa** is the whole diagnosis: malaria until three films say otherwise.
In Nigeria the female **Anopheles** mosquito carries mostly **P. falciparum**, the most dangerous species.

steps.text: People visiting friends and relatives (**VFR travellers**) like Femi often skip prophylaxis because they think they are immune. Immunity fades after leaving an endemic area.

points: No neck stiffness, no rash, chest clear.

steps.lead: Femi has the classic picture: **cyclical fevers with rigors**, headache, myalgia, GI upset, mild jaundice and **hepatosplenomegaly**.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Femi?
steps.r: Fever with rigors, splenomegaly and jaundice after sub-Saharan Africa is **malaria**. Dengue gives a rash and retro-orbital pain; typhoid a slower fever with rose spots.

steps.lead: Femi has falciparum risk, so we watch for **severe** features: glucose below 2.2, falling GCS, acidosis, AKI, severe anaemia.
His film will show **ring-shaped inclusions** if it is falciparum; vivax would be the species that relapses months later.

steps.text: No splenomegaly does not rule out falciparum: it may be absent **early**, and the fever is often **irregular**, not neatly cyclical.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (thick and thin blood films) and what to do if the first film is negative (repeat up to 3 times over 24 to 48 hours).

steps.q: Which test will confirm Femi's diagnosis?
steps.r: **Thick and thin blood film microscopy** is the gold standard: thick for parasite load, thin for species.

steps.lead: Femi's **thick film** counts the parasites and the **thin film** names the species.

visual.title: Parasitaemia on thick film
visual.label: Femi 1.4%
visual.caption: Below 2% on admission: treated as uncomplicated for now.

steps.lead: Alongside the films, Femi needs **FBC, U&Es and glucose**: low platelets and low glucose are common.

steps.title: Femi's admission bloods
steps.text: **Thrombocytopenia** with a normal white count is very typical. Glucose and kidneys are fine for now.

steps.title: If the first film is negative
nodes: Repeat film: up to 3 times over 24–48 h
steps.caption: One negative film never rules out malaria.

steps.text: A normal white count and no splenomegaly do not exclude malaria. **Only three negative films** over 24 to 48 hours do.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': ACT for uncomplicated falciparum, IV artesunate for severe falciparum, chloroquine then primaquine for vivax and ovale.

steps.lead: Femi has uncomplicated **falciparum**, so he starts oral **ACT** (artemisinin-based combination therapy) straight away.

points: 8 hours later: Femi is **drowsy and confused**.

visual.title: Capillary glucose
visual.label: Femi 1.9
visual.caption: Below 2.2 mmol/L is a severe malaria feature. Treat the glucose now too.

steps.q: Femi now has severe falciparum malaria. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
steps.r: Severe falciparum needs prompt parenteral **IV artesunate** with ICU-level care. Chloroquine is for vivax and ovale; primaquine kills liver hypnozoites.

steps.lead: Femi goes to **ICU** for **IV artesunate**. Exchange transfusion is kept as a second-line option.

visual.title: Femi on IV artesunate
visual.caption: Parasites fall quickly on artesunate; daily films track the response.

steps.lead: Falciparum has no hypnozoites, so Femi needs no **primaquine**. Next trip, **doxycycline** prophylaxis would protect him.
Femi's treatment follows WHO guidance; his next trip follows UKHSA prevention advice: bite avoidance and prophylaxis.

steps.text: Do not give **chloroquine** for falciparum: resistance is widespread. Chloroquine is for non-resistant **vivax and ovale**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why vivax and ovale relapse (hypnozoites), why falciparum causes cerebral malaria (sequestration), or why fevers are cyclical.

steps.lead: A mosquito bite in Lagos injected **sporozoites** into Femi; they matured in his liver before invading his red cells.

steps.title: Life cycle in Femi
steps.caption: The liver stage explains why symptoms start at least a week after the bite.

steps.lead: Femi's red cells bursting explains his **jaundice**, falling haemoglobin and enlarged spleen.
Femi's confusion came from infected red cells **sticking to brain capillary endothelium** (cytoadherence and sequestration).

steps.q: Which mechanism best explains Femi's confusion?
o: Sequestration of infected red cells in cerebral microvessels
steps.r: Falciparum-infected cells **cytoadhere** to endothelium and block cerebral microvessels. Hypnozoites belong to vivax and ovale.

steps.lead: Femi's glucose fell because the parasites **consumed glucose** and his liver could not make enough. Quinine would worsen it by releasing insulin.
Had Femi caught **vivax or ovale**, dormant liver **hypnozoites** could have woken months later, so primaquine would be needed.

mcq.q: Which Plasmodium species causes the most severe disease?
mcq.r: **P. falciparum**: cerebral malaria, AKI and highest mortality.
The **female Anopheles** mosquito. Aedes spreads dengue.

mcq.q: Which blood glucose defines severe malaria?
mcq.r: Hypoglycaemia **<2.2 mmol/L** is a severe feature.

mcq.q: What does P. falciparum look like on a thin blood film?
o: Enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots
mcq.r: **Ring-shaped inclusions.** Schüffner's dots and enlarged cells suggest vivax or ovale.

mcq.q: Which is the gold-standard test for malaria?
mcq.r: **Thick and thin film microscopy**: thick for load, thin for species.

mcq.q: How many negative films are needed before ruling out malaria?
mcq.r: Repeat **up to 3 times over 24 to 48 hours**.

mcq.q: Which is first-line for severe P. falciparum malaria?
mcq.r: **IV artesunate** with ICU-level care; exchange transfusion is second-line.

mcq.q: Which drug clears liver hypnozoites to prevent relapse?
mcq.r: **Primaquine**, given after the acute course for vivax and ovale.

mcq.q: Which is first-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum?
Why do P. vivax and P. ovale relapse?
mcq.r: **Hypnozoites** in the liver can reactivate months to years later.

prompts.q: What causes malaria, how is it spread, and which species matter?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the parasite, the vector and the deadly species.

points.p: Plasmodium parasite
points.why: A protozoan, not a bacterium or virus.

points.p: Female Anopheles mosquito
P. falciparum: most common and most dangerous
points.why: Causes almost all severe and fatal malaria.

points.p: P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation of malaria, including the examination findings.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever + travel history + low platelets.

points.p: Fever in a traveller returning from an endemic area (sub-Saharan Africa)
points.why: Travel history is the single most important clue.

points.p: Cyclical fevers with rigors and night sweats
points.why: Falciparum fever is often irregular instead.

points.p: Headache, myalgia, malaise, vomiting, diarrhoea
points.why: GI symptoms can mislead you towards gastroenteritis.

points.p: Hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice
points.why: Splenomegaly may be absent early in falciparum.

points.p: Tachycardia; reduced consciousness if severe
points.why: Any neurological sign makes it severe.

prompts.q: What are the features of severe malaria?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: any one makes it severe and changes treatment to IV artesunate.

points.p: Hypoglycaemia below 2.2 mmol/L
points.why: Check glucose in every drowsy malaria patient.

points.p: Reduced consciousness / cerebral malaria / any neurological symptom
Renal failure (AKI)
Severe anaemia and metabolic acidosis
points.why: From haemolysis and poor tissue perfusion.

points.p: High fever above 39°C; parasitaemia 2% or more

prompts.q: How do the Plasmodium species differ on film and in behaviour?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: rings = falciparum; relapse = vivax or ovale.

points.p: P. falciparum: ring-shaped inclusions on film
points.why: The classic thin film description in stems.

points.p: Falciparum: severe disease, irregular fever, may lack splenomegaly early
points.why: Do not wait for a cyclical pattern.

points.p: P. vivax and ovale relapse due to liver hypnozoites
points.why: Fever months after travel suggests vivax or ovale.

prompts.q: Which test confirms malaria, what does each part show, and what if it is negative?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: thick counts, thin names.

points.p: Thick and thin blood films (microscopy): gold standard
points.why: Not blood cultures, which are for typhoid.

points.p: Thick film: parasite burden (uncomplicated if below 2%)
Thin film: identifies the species
If negative, repeat up to 3 times over 24–48 hours
points.why: Only three negatives rule it out.

prompts.q: Which other first-line bloods do you send, and what do they typically show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: low platelets in a febrile traveller is a malaria clue.

points.p: FBC: anaemia and thrombocytopenia
U&Es: kidney injury
Glucose: hypoglycaemia

prompts.q: How do you treat malaria by species and severity?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity first, then species.

points.p: Severe falciparum: IV artesunate, admit, ICU-level care
Exchange transfusion second-line in select severe cases
Uncomplicated falciparum: ACT
Chloroquine-resistant falciparum: atovaquone-proguanil
Non-resistant vivax/ovale: oral chloroquine

prompts.q: How do you prevent relapse and prevent malaria in travellers?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: primaquine is for the liver, doxycycline for the trip.

points.p: Primaquine after the acute course for vivax/ovale
Doxycycline prophylaxis against falciparum
Bite avoidance (nets, repellent)

prompts.q: Describe the life cycle that causes cyclical fevers, and why vivax and ovale relapse.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: liver first, then red cells.

points.p: Sporozoites injected by the female Anopheles
points.why: The infective stage from the mosquito.

points.p: Liver: mature into merozoites (liver schizogony)
Merozoites invade red cells; cyclical haemolysis causes periodic fevers
points.why: Synchronised rupture gives the fever spikes.

points.p: Vivax and ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites

prompts.q: Why is falciparum so dangerous, and why does severe malaria cause jaundice and hypoglycaemia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sticky cells, burst cells, hungry parasites.

points.p: Cytoadherence: infected red cells stick to endothelium and sequester in microvessels
points.why: Explains cerebral malaria and renal failure.

points.p: Haemolysis releases haemoglobin breakdown products: jaundice, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly
Hypoglycaemia: parasite glucose consumption and impaired gluconeogenesis
Quinine causes insulin release

glossary.malaria: Parasitic infection of red blood cells by Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
glossary.Plasmodium: The protozoan parasite that causes malaria.
glossary.P. falciparum: The most common and most dangerous malaria species; causes cerebral malaria.
glossary.P. vivax: Malaria species that forms liver hypnozoites and can relapse.
glossary.P. ovale: Malaria species that, like vivax, forms hypnozoites and can relapse.
glossary.P. malariae: Less common malaria species causing milder disease.
glossary.Anopheles: Genus of mosquito whose females transmit malaria.
glossary.sub-Saharan Africa: Africa south of the Sahara; where most falciparum malaria is caught.
glossary.rigors: Violent shaking with a feeling of cold as the temperature rises.
glossary.splenomegaly: Enlarged spleen; may be absent early in falciparum malaria.
glossary.jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin; here from red cell breakdown.
glossary.thrombocytopenia: Low platelet count; a common clue to malaria in a febrile traveller.
glossary.parasitaemia: Percentage of red blood cells containing parasites; 2% or more suggests severe disease.
glossary.thick film: Blood film that concentrates cells to detect parasites and count the burden.
glossary.thin film: Blood film spread in a single layer to identify the Plasmodium species.
glossary.ring-shaped inclusions: Ring forms inside red cells on a film; typical of P. falciparum.
glossary.hypnozoites: Dormant liver stages of vivax and ovale that can reactivate months later.
glossary.sporozoites: Infective stage injected by the mosquito; travels to the liver.
glossary.merozoites: Stage released from the liver or burst red cells that invades new red cells.
glossary.schizogony: Asexual multiplication of the parasite, first in the liver then in red cells.
glossary.cytoadherence: Falciparum-infected red cells sticking to blood vessel walls.
glossary.sequestration: Infected red cells trapped in small vessels of the brain, kidney and other organs.
glossary.cerebral malaria: Severe falciparum malaria with reduced consciousness, confusion or seizures.
glossary.severe malaria: Malaria with organ dysfunction, e.g. glucose below 2.2, reduced GCS, AKI, acidosis or severe anaemia.
glossary.ACT: Artemisinin-based combination therapy; first-line for uncomplicated falciparum.
glossary.artesunate: Artemisinin drug given IV as first-line treatment for severe falciparum malaria.
glossary.artemisinin: Fast-acting antimalarial drug class from sweet wormwood.
glossary.chloroquine: Antimalarial for non-resistant vivax and ovale; falciparum is often resistant.
glossary.primaquine: Drug that kills liver hypnozoites to prevent vivax and ovale relapse.
glossary.doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic used as malaria prophylaxis against falciparum.
glossary.quinine: Older antimalarial; causes insulin release and hypoglycaemia.
glossary.exchange transfusion: Removing the patient's blood while replacing it with donor blood; second-line in select severe cases.
glossary.prophylaxis: Medicine taken to prevent a disease, here before, during and after travel.
glossary.VFR: Visiting friends and relatives: travellers at high risk because they often skip prophylaxis.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury; a severe malaria feature.
glossary.UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency; publishes UK malaria prevention guidance.
glossary.haemolysis: Breakdown of red blood cells, releasing haemoglobin.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 2 day history of fever, headache and vomiting. She returned from a 2 week holiday in Uganda 9 days ago. She did not take prophylaxis. Her temperature is 39.6°C. A thin blood film shows red cells containing ring-shaped inclusions, some with two rings in one cell.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: An organism question: travel, timing and the film decide the species.

clues: returned from a 2 week holiday in Uganda 9 days ago
steps.x: Sub-Saharan Africa, short incubation, no prophylaxis, **ring forms** on film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Plasmodium falciparum.**

elim: P. malariae is less common and milder; ring forms with multiple rings per cell point to falciparum.
P. ovale often presents months later and relapses from hypnozoites.
P. vivax is less common in sub-Saharan Africa and relapses.
Typhoid does not show parasites on a blood film.

steps.x: **A. P. falciparum.** Rule: sub-Saharan Africa + ring inclusions = falciparum.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man with P. falciparum malaria on the ward becomes sweaty, agitated and then drowsy 6 hours after admission. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. His parasitaemia on admission was 4%.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?

steps.x: 'Immediate' investigation: the quick bedside test that changes management now.
Severe falciparum with a falling conscious level and sweating: **hypoglycaemia** until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Capillary blood glucose** now (severe if below 2.2).

elim: Cultures look for co-infection but do not explain drowsiness now.
CT head is not first; a reversible cause must be checked at the bedside.
LP is unsafe and slow in a drowsy patient; check glucose first.
Films track response but will not explain acute drowsiness this minute.

steps.x: **B. Capillary glucose.** Rule: drowsy in malaria = check glucose first.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman has fevers every 48 hours for a week. She returned from Pakistan 4 months ago. Thin film shows enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots, identified as Plasmodium vivax from a chloroquine-sensitive area. Parasitaemia is 0.5%. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Glucose and renal function are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

steps.x: Initial treatment: severity, then species.

clues: Plasmodium vivax from a chloroquine-sensitive area
Glucose and renal function are normal
steps.x: Uncomplicated, non-resistant **vivax**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral chloroquine**, then primaquine afterwards.

elim: Atovaquone-proguanil is for chloroquine-resistant falciparum.
Doxycycline is prophylaxis, not treatment of acute vivax.
IV artesunate is for severe falciparum; she has no severe features.
Primaquine clears hypnozoites after the acute course; it does not treat blood-stage disease alone.

steps.x: **D. Oral chloroquine.** Rule: vivax/ovale = chloroquine, then primaquine.

technique.stem: A 40 year old man was treated for P. ovale malaria with chloroquine 8 months ago after a trip to Ghana and his symptoms resolved. He did not complete any further treatment. He has not travelled since. He now has fever and rigors again. His pulse rate is 104 bpm. Blood film shows P. ovale.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his new illness?
o: New infection from a UK mosquito
Sequestration of parasites in the spleen

steps.x: A mechanism question: why has the same species come back?

clues: did not complete any further treatment
steps.x: Ovale, no primaquine, no new exposure, months later: **relapse**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dormant **hypnozoites** in the liver have reactivated.

elim: Resistance would cause early treatment failure, not a relapse 8 months later.
Malaria is not transmitted by mosquitoes in the UK.
Sequestration is a falciparum feature in microvessels, not a cause of late relapse.
Nothing suggests a transfusion.

steps.x: **C. Hypnozoite reactivation.** Rule: vivax/ovale relapse without primaquine.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 4 day history of fever, rigors, headache and aching muscles. She returned from visiting family in Ghana 12 days ago. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her spleen tip is palpable. There is no rash or neck stiffness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever with rigors, splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia 12 days after sub-Saharan Africa is malaria. Dengue gives a rash and retro-orbital pain; typhoid has a slower rising fever.

steps.x: Diagnosis of fever: the travel history first.

clues: fever, rigors, headache and aching muscles
returned from visiting family in Ghana 12 days ago
steps.x: Sub-Saharan Africa, rigors, **splenomegaly**, low platelets, normal white count.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Malaria.**

elim: Dengue usually has a rash and retro-orbital pain; malaria is commoner from West Africa.
Glandular fever gives sore throat and lymphadenopathy in a younger patient.
Influenza does not give splenomegaly and low platelets after Africa.
Typhoid gives a stepwise fever, abdominal pain and rose spots.

steps.x: **D. Malaria.** Rule: fever + Africa + low platelets = malaria until three films say no.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man has had fevers every second day for a week, each with shaking chills followed by sweating. He returned from 6 months working in rural India 5 months ago. He took prophylaxis while there. His temperature is 38.8°C and pulse rate 102 bpm. Thin film shows enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Fever every 48 hours presenting months after travel to South Asia, with enlarged red cells, is P. vivax from reactivated hypnozoites. Falciparum shows ring inclusions and presents within weeks.

steps.x: Organism question: timing and film features decide the species.

clues: enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots
steps.x: Late presentation from South Asia, 48-hour cycle, enlarged cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypnozoite relapse: **P. vivax**.

elim: Falciparum presents within weeks, shows ring inclusions and has no hypnozoites.
P. malariae gives a 72-hour cycle and does not enlarge red cells.
Typhoid shows no parasites on film.
Trypanosomiasis is African sleeping sickness.

steps.x: **C. P. vivax.** Rule: months after travel + enlarged cells = vivax relapse.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has P. falciparum malaria diagnosed on blood film after a trip to Cameroon. He is alert and orientated. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which additional finding would most indicate severe malaria?
practice.e: Hypoglycaemia below 2.2 mmol/L is a severe malaria feature and changes treatment to IV artesunate. Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly are common in uncomplicated malaria.

steps.x: A severity finding: which option is on the severe malaria list?
Currently uncomplicated falciparum (parasitaemia below 2%, alert, normal creatinine).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe features: glucose **<2.2**, reduced consciousness, AKI, acidosis, severe anaemia, fever >39°C.

elim: A mildly raised ALT is common and not a severe criterion.
Splenomegaly is a classic finding in uncomplicated malaria.
Thrombocytopenia is common and not a severe criterion on its own.
38.9°C is below the >39°C threshold in the notes.

steps.x: **B. Glucose 1.9 mmol/L.** Rule: glucose below 2.2 = severe malaria.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man is brought in after a generalised seizure. He returned from Malawi 2 weeks ago and has had fevers for 4 days. He is drowsy with a GCS of 10. There is no neck stiffness or rash. His temperature is 40.2°C, pulse rate 130 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 4.6 mmol/L. Thin film shows ring-shaped inclusions in 9% of red cells.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Seizure and reduced consciousness with falciparum ring forms and normal glucose is cerebral malaria, the key severe complication. Meningitis would usually give neck stiffness.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a returned traveller with a brain problem.

clues: ring-shaped inclusions in 9% of red cells
steps.x: Falciparum, high parasitaemia, reduced GCS, glucose normal so not hypoglycaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cerebral malaria** (severe falciparum).

elim: No neck stiffness or rash, and the film explains everything.
HSV encephalitis does not show parasites on film.
Japanese encephalitis is an Asian virus; he was in Malawi.
Reduced consciousness and seizures make it severe, not uncomplicated.

steps.x: **B. Cerebral malaria.** Rule: falciparum + any neurological sign = cerebral (severe) malaria.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 3 day history of fever and rigors after returning from Sierra Leone. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. She has mild scleral icterus. Her thick blood film is positive for malaria parasites.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
practice.e: Haemolysis and parasite clearance enlarge the liver and spleen, so hepatosplenomegaly is the classic finding in malaria. A palpable gallbladder with jaundice suggests pancreatic cancer.

steps.x: An examination finding for a confirmed malaria patient.
Malaria with jaundice from **haemolysis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hepatosplenomegaly.**

elim: Ascites suggests liver failure or malignancy.
Caput medusae is portal hypertension in cirrhosis.
Courvoisier's sign suggests pancreatic or biliary cancer.
A pulsatile mass is an aortic aneurysm.

steps.x: **C. Hepatosplenomegaly.** Rule: malaria = big liver and spleen, jaundice if severe.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man has fever, dark urine and yellow eyes 10 days after returning from a business trip to Nigeria. He took no prophylaxis. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. He has no rash.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, haemolysis (anaemia, unconjugated bilirubin, high LDH) and thrombocytopenia after West Africa without prophylaxis is falciparum malaria. Hepatitis A gives a much higher ALT.

steps.x: Diagnosis: jaundice in a febrile returned traveller.

clues: 10 days after returning from a business trip to Nigeria
steps.x: Haemolytic pattern, very low platelets, West Africa, no prophylaxis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe **falciparum malaria** with haemolysis.

elim: Hepatitis A gives a hepatitic picture with ALT in the thousands.
G6PD haemolysis needs a trigger and does not cause high fever and low platelets.
Leptospirosis follows freshwater exposure, with conjunctival suffusion and AKI.
Yellow fever gives a hepatitic picture; malaria is far commoner.

steps.x: **D. Falciparum malaria.** Rule: fever + haemolysis + low platelets after Africa = malaria.

practice.stem: A 22 year old student has a 2 day history of fever and headache. She returned from a volunteering trip to Tanzania 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. She has mild splenomegaly.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Thick and thin blood film microscopy is the gold standard for malaria: thick for parasite burden, thin for species. Blood cultures are for typhoid.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: the gold standard for the most likely diagnosis.

clues: returned from a volunteering trip to Tanzania 3 weeks ago
steps.x: Fever after sub-Saharan Africa with splenomegaly and low platelets: malaria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thick and thin blood films.**

elim: Blood cultures diagnose typhoid or bacteraemia, not malaria.
Dengue serology is for dengue, less likely from East Africa with splenomegaly.
Monospot tests for glandular fever.
Urine antigens are for Legionella and pneumococcus.

steps.x: **D. Thick and thin films.** Rule: thick counts, thin names the species.

practice.stem: A 41 year old man has fever and rigors 2 weeks after returning from Kenya. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. A thick and thin blood film taken 2 hours ago shows no parasites. He remains febrile and there is no other source of infection.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
o: Repeat blood films over the next 24 to 48 hours
practice.e: One negative film does not exclude malaria; repeat up to 3 times over 24 to 48 hours. Discharging him after one negative film risks missing falciparum.

steps.x: Next investigation after a negative test.
Suspicion remains high (Africa, low platelets) despite one negative film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Repeat the films**, up to 3 times over 24 to 48 hours.

elim: Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not part of malaria work-up.
CT looks for an abscess, but there is no localising sign.
One negative film cannot rule out malaria.
Ferritin does not diagnose malaria.

steps.x: **D. Repeat films.** Rule: three negative films over 24 to 48 h before ruling out malaria.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Ghana. She is alert and eating. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/76 mmHg and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. Parasitaemia is 0.8%. She is not pregnant.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Uncomplicated falciparum (alert, parasitaemia below 2%, normal glucose and kidneys) is treated with oral ACT. IV artesunate is for severe malaria; chloroquine is for non-resistant vivax and ovale.

steps.x: Initial management: decide severity first.
Falciparum with no severe features: **uncomplicated**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral **ACT**.

elim: Exchange transfusion is second-line in select severe cases.
IV artesunate is for severe malaria.
Falciparum is widely chloroquine-resistant.
Primaquine is for vivax and ovale hypnozoites.

steps.x: **A. ACT.** Rule: uncomplicated falciparum = ACT; severe = IV artesunate.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Nigeria. He has become confused. His temperature is 40.0°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Confusion, AKI, acidosis and high parasitaemia make this severe falciparum malaria: admit, ICU-level care and prompt IV artesunate. Exchange transfusion is only second-line.

steps.x: Initial management: is it severe?
Confusion, fever above 39°C, high parasitaemia, AKI, acidosis: **severe**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV artesunate** with ICU-level care.

elim: Oral atovaquone-proguanil is for uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant falciparum.
Exchange transfusion is second-line in select severe cases.
Oral ACT is for uncomplicated malaria; a confused patient needs parenteral therapy.
Chloroquine is for non-resistant vivax and ovale.

steps.x: **C. IV artesunate.** Rule: severe falciparum = parenteral artesunate first.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has completed a course of oral chloroquine for P. ovale malaria acquired in Nigeria. Her fever has settled and repeat blood film is negative. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her G6PD level is normal.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: P. ovale leaves dormant liver hypnozoites, so primaquine is given after the acute course to prevent relapse (after checking G6PD). Doxycycline is prophylaxis before travel, not hypnozoite treatment.

steps.x: Next step after successful acute treatment.

clues: completed a course of oral chloroquine
steps.x: Ovale, blood stage cleared, G6PD normal so primaquine is safe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Primaquine** to clear hypnozoites.

elim: Doxycycline is prophylaxis against falciparum, not a hypnozoite drug.
IV artesunate is for severe falciparum.
Stopping now leaves hypnozoites that can relapse.
The blood stage is cleared; chloroquine does not reach the liver stage.

steps.x: **D. Primaquine.** Rule: vivax/ovale = chloroquine, then primaquine.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man with P. falciparum malaria becomes unresponsive and has a seizure. His temperature is 40.3°C, pulse rate 134 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and CSF examination is normal. Parasitaemia is 11%.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his reduced consciousness?
o: Sequestration of infected red cells in cerebral microvessels
practice.e: Falciparum-infected red cells cytoadhere to endothelium and sequester in cerebral microvessels, causing cerebral malaria. Glucose and CSF are normal, so hypoglycaemia and meningitis are excluded.

steps.x: Mechanism of the brain problem in falciparum.
Cerebral malaria with glucose and CSF normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cytoadherence and sequestration** in brain capillaries.

elim: CSF is normal, so not meningitis.
Plasmodium infects red cells and liver cells, not neurons.
Hypnozoites belong to vivax and ovale and cause relapse, not coma.
Glucose is normal and no quinine was mentioned.

steps.x: **E. Sequestration.** Rule: falciparum = sticky red cells blocking microvessels.
